commentary.headline: xs-rs wins the small-tree race but real-projects exposes a large gap
paragraphs: The day's scoreboard is clear: xs-rs beat xs-c++ in 10 of 12 contested cells, but both losses are on real-projects. On real-projects fresh, xs-rs took 42.805s against 29.298s for xs-c++ (1.461x slower) and 20.055s for rsync (2.134x slower); on noop it took 2.983s against 1.793s for xs-c++ (1.664x slower), although it still beat rsync at 0.791x. Those are not marginal misses, and they make real-projects the tuning priority. The small-tree wins are real but mostly narrower: laikav2 and congress cells range from about 5% to 15% ahead of xs-c++, with the laikav2 update-10pct cell at 0.949 close to a tie. That contrast matters more than the headline 10-2 score.

Fresh-copy tests point to worker count more than whole-file or compression. In the fresh pin run, -j2 at 1.029s beat -j4 at 1.137s and xs-c++ at 1.143s, while -j2 -z at 1.056s was slightly slower than -j2. The j2W fresh run found -j2 and -j2W effectively tied, at 1.055s and 1.059s, so whole-file was not additive once workers dropped; a separate -j4 whole-file run improved 1.124s to 1.092s, a 2.8% gain but still not a clear 0.90 ratio to xs-c++. On update-10pct, plain -j4 was fastest at 0.437s, level-1 compression was 0.439s, and default -z was 0.454s; -j2 -z matched -j4 on time (0.448s vs 0.451s) while cutting client CPU from 0.090s to 0.067s. These are single-run medians, so treat them as candidates, not defaults.

The sentinel adds a caution: its repeated xs arm ran 4.6% slower than baseline and rsync was 17.7% faster, on only three blocks, while xs burned 7.49 CPU seconds against rsync's 1.94 on real-projects noop. That is not the contest setup, but it warns that run noise can rival the small fresh and update effects and that real-projects CPU behaviour deserves attention. Confidence is provisional: 3 to 12 paired blocks, one direction, warm cache, no significance tests.

Small-tree wins were mostly narrower, down to a 0.949 near-tie on laikav2 update-10pct. Fresh tests suggest two workers help more than whole-file, and compression did not add speed. These are provisional medians, not proven defaults, and real-projects is the clear next tuning target.

Repeat fresh j2 versus j2z versus j4 in one controlled design with at least 12 blocks, and test whether whole-file adds anything after j2.

commentary.headline: xs-rs takes 10 of 12 cells, but real-projects remains a two-cell hole
paragraphs: The day's scoreboard reads 10-2 for xs-rs over xs-c++, with no ties and nothing pending, and both losses are the same corpus twice: real-projects over the a-aws link. Everywhere else xs-rs's time sits between 0.85 and 0.95 of xs-c++'s, and outside real-projects fresh it also beats rsync. On real-projects fresh it took 42.8 s against xs-c++'s 29.3 s and rsync's 20.1 s, so it is 46% slower than its rival and more than twice as slow as the yardstick. On real-projects noop it is 66% slower than xs-c++ (2.98 s vs 1.79 s) yet still 21% faster than rsync. Those two cells alone set the tuning agenda.

The wins cluster where files are small and mostly unchanged. On congress-sample fresh, xs-rs at four workers came in at 2.82 s and 2.95 s across two separate runs while xs-c++ sat near 3.34 s, and it used roughly two thirds of xs-c++'s client CPU; on congress update-10pct it took 0.98 s against 1.17 s for xs-c++ and 1.48 s for rsync. That is a repeated edge rather than one lucky block, though every win still rests on four to eight paired blocks and the ratios carry no intervals.

Two tuning ideas got a cool reception. Adding compression and dropping to two workers on congress fresh was 7% slower than the four-worker default and only about 1% ahead of rsync, so a two-worker-plus-compression small-file default is not supported. On laikav2, two workers gave a 1.8% edge on low-churn updates (0.393 s vs 0.400 s) and was 1.3% slower on high churn, so no universal worker setting follows. The sentinel is the caution: its two near-identical arms differed by 1.7% in median time, yet the paired speed ratio for the second arm against the control read 1.11, a reminder that these ratios are noisy at three blocks.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: xs-rs wins ten of twelve scored cells against xs-c++, and it beats rsync everywhere except real-projects fresh, where it is 2.1x slower than rsync and 46% slower than xs-c++. Its edge is largest on small-file update workloads, where it also uses about half of xs-c++'s client CPU. Adding compression plus two workers did not help small-file fresh copies, and the two-worker advantage on low-churn updates shrank to under 2%. The real-projects losses are the provisional priority for the next round.

commentary.headline: xs-rs leads the race 10–2, but both losses sit on the one large fresh tree
paragraphs: The scoreboard reads 10 cells to xs-rs against 2 for xs-c++, and xs-rs wins wherever the work is incremental or small-file. The widest margin of the day is congress-sample update-1pct: 0.7966 s durable for xs-rs against 0.89465 s for xs-c++ and 1.7886 s for rsync, about 2.2x the control. The narrowest is laikav2 fresh at 0.925 of xs-c++. Both losses are on real-projects, the only big non-incremental tree: fresh took 42.805 s against xs-c++'s 29.298 s and rsync's 20.055 s (1.461 and 2.134), and noop 2.983 s against 1.793 s, though still ahead of rsync's 3.77 s. Cheap incremental work and expensive large-tree fresh work is the day's real signal.

The surprise was compression. The working assumption was that -z would be neutral or harmful where per-file costs dominate; instead congress-sample fresh at -j4 -z finished in 2.72205 s against 3.11545 s for plain -j4, 12.6% faster with client CPU essentially unchanged (2.0175 s vs 2.0145 s), and laikav2 fresh preferred -j2 -z at 1.03355 s over -j4 at 1.12095 s. More workers went the other way: -j8 was 7.9% slower than -j4 on congress fresh (3.0806 s vs 2.85395 s), and -j2 alone was a 1% tie with -j4.

Confidence is capped by the day's own noise floor. The sentinel ran the same xs build twice and got 5.0618 s against 4.2411 s, a 16% gap that blows past the 3% the A/A hypothesis allowed and is wider than the laikav2 (0.925) and laikav2 update-10pct (0.949) wins. Three same-config congress fresh baselines also scattered 2.85–3.12 s. Only within-run pairings, the -z and worker-count comparisons, clear that bar. CPU is a genuine tradeoff: xs-rs is consistently cheaper than xs-c++ on small files (0.4895 s vs 0.982 s on laikav2; 2.0125 s vs 3.0755 s on congress) but spent 9.133 s client CPU against rsync's 2.0 s on real-projects noop. Next: tune the large-tree fresh path, then re-validate -z and worker counts under one roof.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: xs-rs leads the scoreboard 10 cells to 2, winning incremental and small-file cases but losing both real-projects cells, worst on fresh at 42.8 s against xs-c++'s 29.3 s and rsync's 20.1 s. Compression helped small-file fresh copies instead of hurting them (12.6% on congress), and 8 workers were slower than 4. Low worker counts with compression look like promising candidates for small files; the large fresh tree is where tuning is needed. Narrow wins stay provisional because two identical sentinel arms varied by about 16%.

insights.caveat: The two real-projects cells come from experiments whose run detail is not in today's run set, and their absolutes do not match the in-window sentinel real-projects noop (5.06 s for xs), so the size of the gap is scoreboard-level, not a same-day measurement.
insights.evidence: Contest score xs-rs 10, xs-cpp 2. update-1pct run: xs-rs 0.7966 s, xs-cpp 0.89465 s, rsync 1.7886 s (4 blocks each). real-projects fresh: 42.805 s / 29.298 s / 20.055 s (rs_vs_cpp 1.461, rs_vs_rsync 2.134); real-projects noop: 2.983 s / 1.793 s / 3.77 s (rs_vs_cpp 1.664, rs_vs_rsync 0.791).
insights.finding: xs-rs takes 10 of 12 scoreboard cells. Its widest win is congress-sample update-1pct at roughly 2.2x rsync and 0.89 of xs-c++; its thinnest are laikav2 update-10pct (0.949) and laikav2 fresh (0.925). Both losses are on real-projects: fresh at 42.805 s against xs-c++'s 29.298 s and rsync's 20.055 s, and noop at 2.983 s against xs-c++'s 1.793 s, which is still 0.791 of rsync.
insights.title: xs-rs wins the race on incremental and small-file work, loses both large-tree cells

insights.caveat: Three blocks per arm; whether the gap is pure noise or order/thermal drift is a hypothesis, not established.
insights.evidence: Sentinel real-projects noop warm: xs 5.0618 s, again 4.2411 s (identical configuration), rsync 3.8795 s; paired speed again vs xs 1.106. insights.title: The A/A sentinel spread is 16%, wider than most of the race margins

insights.caveat: One within-run comparison on a compressible text corpus; bad for incompressible or pre-compressed data, which was not measured.
insights.evidence: Congress-sample fresh warm: xs-rs -j4 3.11545 s / 0.5605 Gb/s / 2.0145 s CPU; xs-rs -j4 -z 2.72205 s / 0.6413 Gb/s / 2.0175 s CPU; xs-c++ -j4 3.4226 s; rsync 3.2893 s. All arms 8 blocks, same run.

That contradicts the expectation that compression is neutral or harmful where per-file costs dominate, and it turns xs-rs's lead over xs-c++ in this cell from 0.946 (plain) to 0.795.
insights.title: Compression is a real lever on small-file fresh, not a neutral one

insights.caveat: A single run and a small 94 MB corpus; the -j4 -z cell that would isolate worker count from compression was not run here.
insights.evidence: laikav2-sample fresh warm: xs-rs -j2 -z 1.03355 s / 0.7275 Gb/s / 0.4895 s CPU; xs-rs -j4 1.12095 s / 0.6708 Gb/s / 0.5685 s CPU; xs-c++ -j4 1.2295 s / 0.982 s CPU; rsync 1.3648 s / 0.644 s CPU. 8 blocks per arm.
insights.finding: On laikav2 fresh, -j2 -z beat plain -j4 by 7.8% (1.03355 s vs 1.12095 s) and used less client CPU (0.4895 s vs 0.5685 s), making it the fastest arm in the cell at 1.296x rsync and 0.841 of xs-c++. The plain -j4 default already beats both competitors here, so this is an incremental gain on a thin cell rather than a reversal.
insights.title: Low workers plus compression edges out the -j4 default on laikav2 fresh

insights.caveat: Different runs and days for -j2, -j4 and -j8, so these are same-corpus observations rather than one controlled sweep, and the 16% A/A spread covers part of the j2-versus-j4 gap.
insights.evidence: Congress fresh, three runs: -j4 2.8516 s (CPU 2.0125 s), -j2 2.8808 s (CPU 1.519 s), -j8 3.0806 s (CPU 2.736 s); same-run -j4 comparators 2.85395 s and 3.11545 s.

The win over xs-c++ is currently paid for in wall time saved rather than CPU avoided on large trees.
insights.title: CPU tradeoff: xs-rs is lean against xs-c++, heavy against rsync on the large tree

insights.caveat: Different revisions, different days, different primary metric (wall_s vs durable_s); this is an inconsistency to investigate, not a measured regression.
insights.evidence: In-window sentinel real-projects noop warm: xs 5.0618 s at 3.374 Gb/s vs rsync 3.8795 s at 4.403 Gb/s (rsync 1.260x faster). Scoreboard real-projects noop: xs-rs 2.983 s vs rsync 3.77 s (rs_vs_rsync 0.791, xs-rs ahead).

Direction of the xs-versus-rsync result flips between sources.
insights.title: The noop path gives contradictory answers across sources

limitations: Every supplied cell is warm cache, sender-side client, a→aws on one link; no cold-cache, receiver-client or alternate-link data exists in this window.

All figures are medians of 3 to 8 blocks with no confidence intervals or significance testing; the 16% spread between two identical sentinel arms is a concrete floor on how small a margin is meaningful.
The two losing scoreboard cells (real-projects fresh and noop) belong to experiments whose run detail is not among the supplied runs, so their numbers cannot be re-derived or checked here.

Congress-sample fresh baselines come from three different runs and revisions; they are same-corpus observations, not one controlled sweep, and the -j2, -j8 and -z arms were each measured against a different baseline sample.
Client CPU is the only resource measured; receiver CPU, disk and network contention, and compression ratio are not reported.
149 samples, 0 invalid, all runs complete, so there is no failure evidence in this window to reason about.
The sentinel arms xs and again use the same binaries and no tuning flags, but arm order and cache history are not reported, so attributing the 16% gap entirely to noise remains a hypothesis.

Then real-projects noop, where xs-rs takes 2.983 s against xs-c++'s 1.793 s (rs_vs_cpp 1.664) even though it stays at 0.791 of rsync; profile the scan/noop path.
Protect the thinnest wins, laikav2 update-10pct (0.949 of xs-c++) and laikav2 fresh (0.925), by re-running with more blocks to separate them from the measured noise floor.
Re-run the sentinel with at least 8 blocks per arm and randomized arm order so the noise floor is estimated rather than inferred from a single 3-block pair.
Run one controlled 2x2 grid of -j2/-j4 against -z off/on on congress-sample fresh to separate compression from worker count, which today come from different runs.
Repeat the real-projects fresh cell both with and without -z, since compression was the biggest lever on small-file fresh and could plausibly narrow the large-tree gap.

commentary.headline: xs-rs wins the small-file race, but real-projects is still the wall
paragraphs: The scoreboard is the headline: xs-rs leads xs-c++ 10 cells to 2, sweeping all five congress and all five laikav2 cells with time ratios from 0.851 to 0.949. The narrowest win is laikav2 update-10pct at 0.949, about 5% ahead, while congress update-0p1 at 0.851 is clearer. The surprise is the shape of the losses: both are real-projects. On fresh, xs-rs takes 42.8 s against 29.3 s for xs-c++ and 20.1 s for rsync, or 1.46x and 2.13x. On noop it takes 2.98 s against 1.79 s for xs-c++, 1.66x, though it still beats rsync at 0.79x. That points to a many-file, large-tree weakness rather than a general transfer problem.

The most actionable pattern is two workers on laikav2. In the fresh 12-block race, -j2 finished in 1.064 s versus 1.173 s for default -j4, about 9% faster, and both beat xs-c++. On update-1pct, -j2 was 0.369 s versus 0.382 s for -j4; on update-0p1, the separate -j2 run was 0.363 s versus 0.400 s for xs-c++, but that run lacked a same-run -j4 control. Compression is not supported at 1pct churn: -z was 0.387 s versus 0.381 s plain, about 1.5% slower, with slightly more CPU.

CPU is a real xs-rs advantage: on fresh it used 0.489 s client CPU at -j2 versus 0.956 s for xs-c++, and on update-0p1 0.046 s versus 0.107 s. The sentinel is a caution: its A/A repeat differed by 1.5%, inside the 3% expectation, yet rsync was 33% faster than xs in that real-projects noop cell. With 8-12 matched blocks and no intervals, -j2 is a candidate, not a proven default; real-projects needs a controlled sweep.

commentary.headline: xs-rs leads the scoreboard, but real-projects is still the clear loss
paragraphs: The day's scoreboard reads xs-rs 10, xs-cpp 2, no ties, so xs-rs has a strong lead across the congress and laikav2 cells. The two losses are both real-projects, and they are not small: on real-projects fresh xs-rs recorded 42.805s against xs-cpp's 29.298s and rsync's 20.055s, ratios of 1.461 and 2.134; on real-projects noop xs-rs recorded 2.983s against xs-cpp's 1.793s, a 1.664 ratio, though it still beat rsync at 0.791. That is the scoreboard's central tension: a broad win pattern with a concentrated, severe weak spot. Because the scoreboard combines separate experiments, it is a map of where to look, not a controlled comparison.

The most useful tuning signal came from laikav2 fresh, where lowering xs-rs from -j4 to -j2 produced 1.058s versus xs-cpp's 1.168s, about 9.5% faster, while default -j4 at 1.191s was about 2.0% slower than xs-cpp. CPU also fell to 0.48s for -j2 against 0.946s for xs-cpp, pointing to worker contention as the lever in this small-file fresh cell. The separate laikav2 fresh compression run tempers the compression story: xs-rs-z at 1.126s was only 0.9% faster than plain xs-rs at 1.136s and about 4.0% faster than xs-cpp, far short of the earlier <=0.90 hypothesis. These are 12-block medians from separate runs, so -j2 is a candidate, not a settled default.

The update-10pct run shows an interaction rather than an additive win: -z at -j4 was fastest at 0.442s versus xs-cpp at 0.479s, while -j8 alone reached 0.462s and adding -z to -j8 slowed it to 0.485s. On congress, xs-rs -j4 beat both tools in fresh (2.948s vs 3.391s xs-cpp and 3.273s rsync) and update (1.032s vs 1.158s and 1.498s), with lower client CPU than xs-cpp. The sentinel's 7.8% A/A drift and the real-projects CPU gap show not every setting effect is stable. Keep -j2 and -z at -j4 as candidates, avoid -j8z on update-10pct, and attack real-projects before calling any of this production guidance.

commentary.headline: xs-rs leads the race, but real-projects is still the wall
paragraphs: The scoreboard now reads xs-rs 10 cells, xs-c++ 2. That is a strong day for the Rust xs, but both losses are real-projects: on fresh, xs-rs takes 1.46 times xs-c++'s time and 2.13 times rsync's; on noop, it takes 1.66 times xs-c++'s time, though it still edges rsync at 0.79 times its time. Those cells matter because they show the win is workload-dependent, not global.

On laikav2 fresh, xs-rs beat xs-c++ by about 9% in an 8-block cell (1.097s versus 1.202s), but the 12-block pin narrowed the ratio to 0.948. The win is real but thin; the earlier 0.895 was optimistic. Adding -z moved xs-rs to 1.065s, about 3% better than xs-rs default and 11% better than xs-c++, but with slightly higher client CPU (0.581s versus 0.555s). No wire-byte data was supplied, so the compression explanation remains a hypothesis.

The worker story is not simple. -j8 was a regression on laikav2 fresh (1.227s versus 1.066s at -j4) and neutral-to-slower on update-1pct (0.379s versus 0.370s), so the update-10pct concurrency gain did not generalize. At update-10pct, -j4 still beat xs-c++ (0.436s versus 0.479s, ratio 0.911) at about half the client CPU (0.082s versus 0.169s). Congress update-1pct was a clear win (0.779s versus 0.848s, and 0.44 times rsync), but only four blocks. Sentinel A/A drift (5.033s versus 4.467s) warns that real-projects noise is high.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. On laikav2 and congress, xs-rs wins by roughly 5 to 15%, with the fresh 12-block result narrowing to a near-tie. Compression -z gives a small fresh gain; -j8 hurts fresh and does not help update-1pct, while -j4 still wins update-10pct with lower CPU. The main open question is why real-projects is slow for xs-rs and whether that is scan, metadata or workload shape.

commentary.headline: xs-rs wins most small-file cells, but real-projects is a clear loss
paragraphs: The day's scoreboard is lopsided in xs-rs's favor: 10 wins to xs-c++'s 2, with no ties or pending cells. The exceptions are the largest real-projects cells. On fresh real-projects, xs-rs took 42.805s versus 29.298s for xs-c++ and 20.055s for rsync (1.461 times xs-c++, 2.134 times rsync). On noop it took 2.983s versus 1.793s for xs-c++, though still ahead of rsync's 3.77s. These are the losses that matter most, and the supplied run list has no detailed BL2-real-projects run to explain them.

In congress and laikav2, xs-rs mostly delivered. It won congress fresh at 2.912s versus 3.4074s for xs-c++ and 3.22335s for rsync, and congress update-10pct at 0.96665s versus 1.1522s and 1.498s. The narrowest win was laikav2 update-0.1pct: 0.3769s versus 0.40135s, a scoreboard ratio of 0.952 that misses the planned 0.95 bar, so it is provisional. On laikav2 update-1pct, xs-rs reached 0.36435s versus 0.40645s for xs-c++ and 0.4742s for rsync over eight matched blocks.

A useful negative result came from raising only xs-rs to -j8 on laikav2 update-10pct: 0.4459s versus 0.4437s at -j4, while client CPU rose from 0.088s to 0.1105s. That does not support more workers as a simple win. The sentinel's A/A ratio of 0.996 suggests low drift in its own setup, but it used an older revision and its xs arm was far slower than rsync on large real-projects noop, so it warns about corpus effects rather than settling the current race. Most congress comparisons rest on four blocks; treat them as screening evidence.

Raising xs-rs from four to eight workers did not improve laikav2 update-10pct and added CPU. The laikav2 update-0.1pct win is narrow and provisional. commentary.headline: xs-rs wins the day 7-2-2, but real-projects is the unresolved loss
paragraphs: The scoreboard says xs-rs 7, xs-c++ 2, tie 2, pending 0. The wins are broad: congress update-1pct (rs_vs_cpp 0.842; xs-rs 0.884s vs xs-c++ 1.05s and rsync 1.774s), laikav2 update-1pct (0.939; 0.386s vs 0.411s), laikav2 fresh (0.869), congress fresh (0.84), and noop cells. The ties are laikav2 update-10pct (0.967; xs-rs 0.469s vs xs-c++ 0.485s) and update-0p1pct (0.987; 0.375s vs 0.38s). The losses are both real-projects cells: noop rs_vs_cpp 1.664 and fresh 1.461, where xs-rs took 42.8s vs xs-c++ 29.3s and rsync 20.1s. That is the day's biggest signal.

Why? On laikav2 updates xs-rs is not winning by brute force: at update-1pct it used 0.0545s client CPU vs xs-c++ 0.1185s, and at update-0p1pct 0.0475s vs 0.11s while tying duration. Congress update-1pct is different: xs-rs used 0.91s CPU, above rsync 0.731s but below xs-c++ 1.1865s. The real-projects sentinel, using older xs, saw rsync 23% faster than xs and xs client CPU 9.01s vs rsync 2.022s, hinting that many-file scan/CPU overhead may explain the contest losses. This is a hypothesis, not a controlled xs-rs result.

Confidence is provisional. Cells have 3 to 8 blocks, medians only, and the sentinel's A/A repeat was 5.6% slower than xs, beyond its 3% drift target. The update-10pct and 0p1pct ties are not losses, but they are not wins either. Keep xs-rs as a strong candidate for congress and laikav2 update/fresh, avoid claiming it as a default, and put real-projects fresh first in the next tuning cycle.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: xs-rs beat xs-c++ in 7 of 11 scored cells, lost both real-projects cells, and tied the two laikav2 update cells. It is ahead on congress and laikav2 updates and fresh, often with lower client CPU than xs-c++. The big hole is real-projects fresh: 42.8s for xs-rs vs 29.3s for xs-c++ and 20.1s for rsync. The sentinel's 5.6% A/A drift and small block counts make these provisional. Next, tune real-projects fresh, then real-projects noop, then the laikav2 update ties.

commentary.headline: xs-rs leads 5-2, but update and large-corpus runs keep the race unsettled
paragraphs: The scoreboard is the day's main story: xs-rs wins five cells to xs-c++'s two. The wins cover congress-sample fresh, noop and update-10pct plus laikav2-sample fresh and noop, with xs-rs/xs-c++ ratios from 0.871 to 0.945. In the clearest detailed runs, xs-rs finished congress fresh in 2.949s versus 3.563s for xs-c++, and congress update in 1.171s versus 1.331s; it also used much less client CPU on several fresh runs (1.878s versus 3.501s). That matters because xs-rs is not merely matching xs-c++; it can beat it while spending fewer client CPU seconds.

The caveat is that the race is not uniform. Update-10pct is the weak spot: three detailed runs show xs-rs at 1.402s versus 1.251s, 1.532s versus 1.233s, and 1.476s versus 1.237s, even though one update run wins at 1.171s versus 1.331s. Congress fresh also has a 3.547s versus 3.403s loss and a near tie, and the scoreboard's two losses are both real-projects, where xs-rs takes 1.461x and 1.664x as long as xs-c++. Confidence is limited: each cell has only two to five blocks, the numbers are medians without significance tests, and revisions differ across runs, so these are not controlled comparisons. reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. xs-rs leads the race on the scoreboard, winning five cells to xs-c++'s two, and it often uses less client CPU. The wins are concentrated in congress-sample fresh/noop and laikav2-sample, where xs-rs is about 10-18% faster in several runs and roughly twice as fast as the rsync reference on congress noop. The losses are real-projects and several update-10pct runs, where xs-rs trails xs-c++ by 12-24% in detailed runs. insights.title: Update-10pct is the main weak spot

commentary.headline: xs-rs stays winless against xs-c++, with a useful update-copy tie and clear metadata-path losses
paragraphs: The day's scoreboard is blunt: xs-cpp takes four of five contest cells, xs-rs wins none, and one cell is a tie. The tie is update-10pct, where xs-rs records 1.613s against xs-c++ at 1.573s, an rs_vs_cpp ratio of 1.025, so essentially parity. Everywhere else xs-rs trails, and on the large real-projects tree the gap is material: 42.805s versus 29.298s on fresh copies, ratio 1.461, and 2.983s versus 1.793s on noop, ratio 1.664. The reference arm, rsync, is faster than both on real-projects fresh at 20.055s, but both xs arms beat it on real-projects noop.

The small-file congress results are more encouraging but less stable. Baseline fresh medians are almost tied: xs-rs 3.4488s, xs-c++ 3.5397s, reference 3.4219s. Yet the later fresh contest cell puts xs-rs at 4.329s against xs-c++ at 3.569s, ratio 1.213, while the run's own paired ratio is about 0.999. Noop tells a similar story: congress noop is 0.852s versus 0.797s, ratio 1.069, and port-step noop runs range from close (0.834s versus 0.765s) to clearly slow (1.705s versus 0.812s). This looks like an unstable metadata or scheduling path rather than a bandwidth ceiling.

CPU does not give xs-rs a clean escape. It uses less client CPU than xs-c++ on fresh congress (2.609s versus 3.749s) despite similar elapsed time, but much more on real-projects fresh (44.77s versus 28.24s) while also running slower. With only two to four matched blocks per cell, different revisions, and only one A-to-AWS warm-cache direction, these are screening signals, not proof. The practical message is to treat update copies as the one credible xs-rs candidate, and to tune and profile xs-rs on real-projects noop and fresh, then congress noop and fresh, before claiming any default.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: xs-rs still trails xs-c++, with no contest wins, one tie on update copies, and clear losses on fresh and noop. The update tie shows parity is reachable on small-file updates, but the real-projects and noop results point to a metadata-path gap. Provisional guidance is to keep the update setting as a candidate, avoid promoting fresh or noop behaviour, and tune xs-rs next on real-projects noop and fresh, then congress noop and fresh. Small matched samples limit confidence.

commentary.headline: xs -j4 reliably halves no-op time, but more workers and fresh copies do not follow
paragraphs: The clearest result of the day is that xs with -j4 was about twice as fast as rsync on congress-sample no-op copies (25,246 files, 218 MB, a to aws, warm cache). Across five runs with four matched blocks each, xs-cpp medians landed at 0.75, 0.78, 0.80, 0.83 and 0.89 s against rsync's 1.54–1.58 s, a paired speed of 1.72× to 2.08×, and it held across two xs revisions. That is the most reproducible signal in the window and it supports treating worker count as the main tuning lever rather than a detail.

The bigger real-projects no-op corpus (69,316 files, 2.13 GB) fills in the mechanism. Serial xs was slower than rsync, 5.43 s against 3.58 s (0.66×), while burning 9.66 s of client CPU against rsync's 1.88 s. With -j4 it flipped to 1.88 s, or 1.93× rsync; with -j8 it only reached 2.73 s, or 1.31×. The day's earlier assumption that -j8 would push xs under 1.10× is therefore not supported, and more workers actually made it worse. That looks like contention or per-file overhead above four workers, though a single run cannot separate the two.

The fresh-transfer arm is the regression to watch. xs took 25.16 s against rsync's 20.21 s (0.80×) and used roughly twice the client CPU, 33.3 s versus 16.6 s, with both tools stuck below 0.85 Gb/s. Confidence is moderate: these are four-block medians without confidence intervals, and the sentinel's A/A repeat agreed within 1.6–2.5% while its rsync-to-xs ratio drifted from 1.32 to 1.50 between hours.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: xs with four workers was consistently about twice as fast as rsync on small-file no-op copies, and the same setting turned a 34% deficit on a larger corpus into a 93% gain, which points to worker count as the lever that matters. More workers did not help: eight workers gave back most of that gain. Fresh copies were slower than rsync and both tools ran under 0.9 Gb/s. The main open question is whether four workers is the real sweet spot or just the best point tested so far.

insights.caveat: Medians of four blocks per arm, no confidence intervals; a single corpus, one direction and a warm cache. Revisions differ between the two experiments, so this is replication, not a controlled version comparison.
insights.finding: On congress-sample no-op, xs with -j4 beat rsync in every complete run of the day, by 1.72× to 2.08× in paired time to durable, with medians of roughly 0.75–0.89 s against rsync's 1.54–1.58 s.
insights.title: xs -j4 is consistently about twice rsync on congress-sample no-op

insights.caveat: One run, 12 blocks per arm, one corpus and direction; the -j8 deficit may be contention, memory pressure or a per-file cost that scales with worker count. Not established as a general ceiling.
insights.evidence: AP10200112-A1-noop-jobs, 69316 files / 2.134 GB, 12 blocks per arm: rsync 3.581 s (1×), serial xs 5.430 s (0.661×), xs-j4 1.883 s (1.930×), xs-j8 2.731 s (1.313×). The run's own hypothesis expected -j8 to bring the ratio below 1.10.
insights.finding: Parallelism, not the tool choice alone, explains the real-projects no-op result: serial xs was 34% slower than rsync, -j4 was 93% faster, and -j8 gave back most of that gain at 1.31×. The stated hypothesis that -j8 would reach below 1.10× rsync is overturned; four workers outperformed eight.
insights.title: Four workers beat eight on the larger corpus; the -j8 hypothesis failed

insights.caveat: Client CPU only, not total system cost; single run, 12 blocks, no profiling of where the CPU goes. Offered as a hypothesis about per-file overhead, not a measured cause.
insights.evidence: AP10200112-A1-noop-jobs, 69316 files / 2.134 GB: serial xs 9.659 s client CPU for 5.430 s wall, rsync 1.884 s for 3.581 s, xs-j4 2.906 s for 1.883 s, xs-j8 4.661 s for 2.731 s. E1 baseline serial xs 9.335 s CPU for 5.244 s against rsync 1.893 s for 3.605 s.
insights.finding: Serial xs spends about five times rsync's client CPU while delivering less throughput, and CPU rises further with worker count while time falls only up to -j4. The default single-worker path looks dominated by per-file or metadata work rather than bandwidth.
insights.title: Serial xs burns CPU without buying speed

insights.caveat: Four blocks per arm in one run, one corpus and one link; the fresh path may be dominated by receiver-side or wire limits that tuning the sender will not move.
insights.evidence: E1-vps-baseline fresh, 69316 files / 2.134 GB: rsync 20.214 s at 0.845 Gb/s and 16.633 s CPU versus xs 25.162 s at 0.679 Gb/s and 33.278 s CPU, paired speed 0.802×, 4 blocks per arm.
insights.finding: On fresh copies of real-projects, xs remained 20% slower than rsync, 25.16 s versus 20.21 s, with double the client CPU, and both tools stayed under 0.85 Gb/s. The no-op advantage does not carry into the fresh path.
insights.title: Fresh transfers are a regression and a throughput ceiling

insights.caveat: Only -j4 is tested in these two experiments; -j8 was fixed in the other run's configuration, and no single run compared workers head to head on this corpus. Different corpora sizes also confound any cross-run parallel-worker reading.
insights.evidence: AP10200112-A1-noop-jobs is the only run with a controlled worker sweep: -j4 1.883 s (1.930×) and 2.906 s CPU; -j8 2.731 s (1.313×) and 4.661 s CPU.
insights.finding: The worker-count effect on real-projects argues for four as the working candidate rather than eight: -j4 delivered 1.93× rsync at 2.91 s CPU, while -j8 delivered only 1.31× and consumed 4.66 s CPU, so extra parallelism cost CPU without buying time.
insights.title: Worker scaling on real-projects: four is the working candidate, not eight

insights.caveat: Small sample, four blocks per run, and the spread may reflect ordering, cache state or host noise rather than a real bimodality; no routing exploration was done.
insights.finding: The xs-rs arm on congress-sample no-op is unstable: paired speed versus rsync ranged from 0.96× to 1.36× across five runs at four blocks each, straddling parity, while the -j4 C++ arm stayed between 1.72× and 2.08×.

insights.caveat: Three blocks per arm and wall_s rather than durable_s, so this cannot be compared directly with the E1 durable-time ratio; only the A/A agreement and the drift are informative.
insights.finding: The hourly A/A control reproduced within 1.6% and 2.5%, staying inside the 3% band, but the rsync-to-xs ratio moved from 1.50 to 1.32 between the two sentinel windows. Repeats are tight; cross-hour comparisons are not.

insights.caveat: One run out of eight contributed the invalid samples, and it is the only witness for the 1.94× figure, so that specific number is the least trustworthy of the day's xs -j4 results.
insights.evidence: FC-02bd268-noop 181617Z: 22 samples with 12 invalid, rsync 6 valid samples over 3 blocks (1.5425 s), xs-cpp 4 valid samples over 3 blocks (0.7818 s); comparable arms absent. The other FC-02bd268 runs reported 12 samples with 0 invalid and blocks of 4.

limitations: All figures are window-only medians with no confidence intervals and no significance testing; differences are described, not established.
Most arms rest on four blocks and a handful of valid samples, so run-to-run spread (as with xs-rs) can exceed the apparent arm difference.
Only one corpus per size class is covered, only the a-to-aws link is exercised, the client is the sender throughout, and the cache is warm in every cell.
Compression, storage target and reverse direction are absent from this window, so none of their interactions can be assessed.
Runs with different worker counts, corpora or scenarios are not controlled comparisons; cross-run readings of the worker effect remain hypotheses.
The AP10200112 and FC-* experiments use different corpora and primaries (wall_s versus durable_s), so their speed ratios are not directly interchangeable.
The sentinel uses wall_s and three blocks, which limits comparison with the E1 durable-time baseline.
nextSteps: Repeat the real-projects no-op worker sweep (-j2, -j4, -j6, -j8, -j16) with more blocks and randomized ordering so the four-versus-eight question is answered as a controlled comparison.
Add a cold-cache and a fresh-path variant of the congress-sample cell to see whether the 2× no-op win survives when the receiver must write full file contents.
Second run of the real-projects fresh cell, with receiver CPU and disk-write time captured, to test whether the 0.80× regression is sender work or a receiver-side ceiling.
Profile serial xs's per-file client CPU (9.66 s against rsync's 1.88 s) to identify which metadata step dominates before the default worker count is changed.

tuningImplications.tradeoffs: The -j4 arm used about 0.89–1.00 s of client CPU against rsync's 0.60–0.64 s for a roughly 2× time saving, so it is a favourable but not free trade. xs-rs moved between 0.96× and 0.97× rsync here, i.e. approximate parity, and cannot be ranked on this sample.

tuningImplications.tradeoffs: xs-rs ranged from parity to 1.36× rsync across runs at four blocks each, so promoting it would be premature; the invalid-sample run also produced three-block medians that should not be compared with four-block medians.

tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Moderate for -j4 over rsync and for -j4 over -j8: one run, but 12 blocks per arm with zero invalid samples. Weak as a general rule on worker count.
tuningImplications.nextTest: Rerun with -j2, -j4, -j6, -j8 and -j16 under randomized ordering and more blocks to locate the actual optimum rather than assuming four.
tuningImplications.recommendation: Support parallel workers as a candidate setting and prefer four over eight; avoid the serial default for large no-op syncs, and do not adopt eight workers.
tuningImplications.tradeoffs: -j4 reached 1.883 s at 2.906 s client CPU; -j8 reached 2.731 s at 4.661 s CPU, so extra workers cost CPU without gaining time. Serial xs was slower than rsync at 9.659 s CPU, the worst CPU-per-byte of any arm here.

tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Provisional: two hourly windows of three blocks each, wall-clock primary, A/A agreement strong but the cross-tool ratio drifted.
tuningImplications.nextTest: Keep the hourly A/A sentinel running and record it alongside durable_s so its ratio can be compared directly with the E1 baseline rather than only within an hour.
tuningImplications.recommendation: Keep the sentinel as a stability check and use it to bound noise; avoid attributing the 1.32 to 1.50 ratio shift to a code or configuration change without a paired check.
tuningImplications.tradeoffs: Repeat runs agreed within 1.6–2.5%, which supports small block-level noise but not cross-hour inference; three blocks per arm and a wall-clock primary limit how far these ratios can be pushed.

tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Weak for a recommendation and moderate as a caution: four blocks per arm in one run, no profile of where the extra CPU goes.
tuningImplications.nextTest: Re-run the fresh cell with receiver-side timing and disk-write accounting, and add a fresh cell at a second corpus size, before changing any fresh-path default.
tuningImplications.recommendation: Avoid presenting xs as a general-purpose replacement for rsync; it is a supported candidate for no-op small-file work only, and the serial default should be treated as an open problem rather than a baseline.
tuningImplications.tradeoffs: On no-op, serial xs was 0.68× rsync (5.244 s against 3.605 s) at roughly five times the client CPU; on fresh, 0.80× (25.162 s against 20.214 s) at double the CPU. commentary.headline: Parallelism helped, but eight workers did not beat four in the warm no-op screen
paragraphs: The most useful surprise came from the worker screen: in one warm no-op cell, baseline xs ran at 0.6614x rsync (5.4304 s vs 3.58095 s), while -j4 reached 1.9296x and -j8 only 1.3132x. The -j4 arm was fastest at 1.8831 s and 9.0701 Gb/s, ahead of rsync's 4.7697 Gb/s; -j8 was 2.7308 s and 6.2545 Gb/s. More jobs were not monotonically better, so four workers is the provisional candidate, not eight. CPU rose from 1.8835 s for rsync to 2.9055 s for -j4 and 4.661 s for -j8, a real tradeoff.

The baseline run supports the single-stream deficit: xs was 0.6806x rsync on no-op and 0.8022x on fresh, with times of 5.2443 vs 3.60535 s and 25.16185 vs 20.2138 s. Fresh also roughly doubled client CPU for xs (33.2775 vs 16.633 s), so the gap is not just wall time. The no-op ratio agrees with the worker screen's 0.6614x baseline across independent runs, which strengthens the direction of the finding, though it is not a controlled replication.

The sentinels showed repeat xs within 1.0247x and 1.0161x, inside the 3% A/A check, but rsync vs xs moved between 1.3213x and 1.4956x on only 3 blocks per arm. Measurement is stable enough for gross screening, not precise ranking. All results are medians without confidence intervals and cover one corpus, one direction, and warm no-op plus fresh cells; treat the four-worker result as promising and validate it on fresh transfers before calling it a default.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: in a warm no-op screen on real-projects a to aws, four parallel workers beat both baseline xs and eight workers; eight helped over baseline but was slower than four. Single-stream xs still trailed rsync and used more CPU, especially on fresh transfers. Hourly A/A checks stayed within about 3%, so gross timing was stable, though the rsync-to-xs gap moved between sentinels. These are provisional medians from small blocks, not production defaults; the worker result needs a controlled fresh-transfer follow-up.

insights.title: Four workers beat eight in the warm no-op screen
insights.finding: Within the same warm no-op cell, xs with -j4 had the lowest median wall time, 1.8831 s, versus 2.7308 s for -j8, 3.58095 s for rsync, and 5.4304 s for baseline xs. Speed vs rsync was 1.9296x for -j4, 1.3132x for -j8, and 0.6614x for baseline xs.
insights.evidence: 12 matched blocks per arm; median throughput was 9.0701 Gb/s for -j4, 6.2545 for -j8, 4.7697 for rsync, and 3.1456 for baseline xs.
insights.caveat: Single no-op warm cell, no fresh scenario, medians only with no confidence intervals; the -j4-over--j8 ordering is an observation from 12 blocks, not a proven optimum.

insights.title: The parallel win carries a CPU cost
insights.finding: Median client CPU was 2.9055 s for -j4 and 4.661 s for -j8, versus 1.8835 s for rsync and 9.6585 s for baseline xs. Thus -j4 roughly halved baseline xs CPU use while beating rsync on wall time and throughput in this cell.
insights.evidence: 12 matched blocks per arm; -j4 delivered 1.8831 s and 9.0701 Gb/s, while rsync delivered 3.58095 s and 4.7697 Gb/s.
insights.caveat: CPU is client-side only in the supplied data; no server CPU, energy, or durability measurement. Medians only, with no confidence intervals.

insights.title: Single-stream xs lags rsync in both baseline scenarios
insights.finding: In the baseline run, xs speed vs rsync was 0.6806x on no-op and 0.8022x on fresh. Median times were 5.2443 s vs 3.60535 s no-op, and 25.16185 s vs 20.2138 s fresh. The no-op xs deficit matches the worker screen's 0.6614x baseline.
insights.evidence: 4 matched blocks per arm per scenario; no-op throughput was 3.2582 vs 4.7374 Gb/s, and fresh throughput was 0.6792 vs 0.8450 Gb/s.
insights.caveat: Independent runs are not a controlled replication; both cover a single corpus, link, direction, and warm cache. The cells are small at 4 blocks.

insights.title: Fresh transfers expose a CPU and throughput gap
insights.finding: Fresh transfers were much slower than no-op in absolute terms, and xs used about twice rsync's median client CPU: 33.2775 s vs 16.633 s. Delivered throughput was 0.6792 Gb/s for xs vs 0.8450 Gb/s for rsync.
insights.evidence: Fresh median durable time was 25.16185 s for xs vs 20.2138 s for rsync, with 4 matched blocks per arm.
insights.caveat: Only one fresh cell; cannot separate metadata, payload, durable-write, and CPU effects. Medians only, no significance testing.

insights.title: A/A sentinels held near parity, but tiny samples limit ranking
insights.finding: Repeat xs vs xs was 1.0247x in one sentinel and 1.0161x in the other, within the stated 3% check. Rsync vs xs was 1.3213x in the first and 1.4956x in the second, showing the rsync-to-xs gap varied between sentinel runs.
insights.evidence: 3 matched blocks per arm per sentinel; median times were 4.3353 s xs, 4.3287 s again, and 3.4336 s rsync in one; 5.4543 s xs, 5.3134 s again, and 3.6231 s rsync in the other.
insights.caveat: Two short sentinels with 3 blocks per arm; A/A stability is gross, not precise. Do not use these to rank tools.

limitations: Medians only; no confidence intervals or significance tests are supplied.
Small matched samples: 12 blocks per arm in the worker screen, 4 in the baseline run, and 3 in each sentinel.
Evidence covers one corpus, real-projects, one direction, a to aws, and a warm cache; no cold-cache, reverse-direction, storage, compression, or file-size interaction data are supplied.
The worker screen tested only no-op; the baseline tested fresh and no-op but with only 4 blocks per arm; sentinels used only 3 blocks per arm.
Cross-run consistency between the worker-screen no-op baseline and the baseline-run no-op result is supportive but not a controlled comparison across runs.
Client CPU is the only CPU measure supplied; tradeoffs against server CPU, network, and durability are not measured.
nextSteps: Run a controlled follow-up with predeclared worker arms around the tested -j4 and -j8, more matched blocks, and both fresh and no-op scenarios in the same cell.
Validate the fresh-transfer gap with cold and warm cache if available, and report wall time, durable time, throughput, and client CPU together.
Increase sentinel block counts to estimate run-to-run noise before using sentinels for thresholds or tool ranking.
Test whether the -j4 advantage holds across additional corpora, directions, and storage types before treating it as a production default.
Keep baseline xs and rsync arms paired in follow-up runs so gains are measured within the same time window.
